utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-05-87/1-I, the Prosecutor versus Vlastimir Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And could I have the appearances from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My name is Tom Hannis. I represent the OTP. I'm assisted today by trial attorney Christina Moeller on my right and on my left our case manager, Susan Grogan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the Prosecution [sic]?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. And my learned friends, I'm Jelena Nikolic. I'm duty counsel currently representing General Vlastimir Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nikolic, and I thank you for your willingness to take care of this matter today. Good afternoon, everyone inside the courtroom and in the gallery. This is the Initial Appearance under Rule 62 of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Initial Appearance of Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic, who was indicted by the Tribunal in October 2003, and who was arrested Sunday last in Montenegro, I understand, and brought here to the Tribunal on that same day. Now, once an accused has been arrested and brought to the seat of the Tribunal, the first thing that has to happen is that the accused must be brought before the Trial Chamber to which the case was assigned by the president or to a Judge of that Chamber, and there, he must make a plea of either guilty or not guilty to the charges raised against him in the indictment. That is the sole purpose of this hearing today and that's all that's going to happen. But before we begin, I'd like to ascertain that you, Mr. Djordjevic, can hear me and understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The first thing I guess I should do is to establish that you are who you are. So I would like you to state your full name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vlastimir Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 17th of November, 1948.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The village of Koznica, Vladicin Han municipality, Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, where did you reside at the time of your arrest? What was your --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Belgrade, Belgrade Battalion 39 is the name of the street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And what was your occupation when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A retiree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And lastly, could you inform us of the name of your father and mother?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My father's name is Stojan. My mother's name is Rusiteva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djordjevic, has your family been informed of your arrest and transfer to the seat of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Pursuant, then, to Article 20 of the statute, I first have to satisfy myself that your rights at this stage of the proceedings have been respected, including your right to be promptly informed of the charges against you and of your right to counsel. These rights are enshrined in Article 21 of the statute and they include the right to a fair and public hearing, the right to be presumed innocent until proven guilty, the right to be informed promptly and in detail in a language you understand of the nature and of the cause of the charges against you, the right to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of your defence, and to communicate with counsel of your own choosing, the right to be tried without undue delay, the right to be tried in your presence and to defend yourself in person or through legal assistance of your own choosing, and to be informed of this right, including the right to have legal counsel assigned to you where the interests of justice so require, and without payment by you, if you have not sufficient means to pay for counsel by yourself, also the right to examine and have examined the witnesses against you at trial and to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on your behalf under the same conditions as those witnesses brought against you, also the right to have free assistance of an interpreter if you do not understand or speak any of the languages which are used in this Tribunal, and finally, the right not to be compelled to testify against yourself or to confess guilt. I have to ask you, Mr. Djordjevic, if you were advised of these rights upon your arrest and if you have received a copy of the indictment. Do you -- did you receive a copy of the indictment and have you been advised of these rights when you were arrested or when you came to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have been informed about all of my rights in accordance with the Statute and yes, I did receive a copy of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's then proceed with your plea to the charges raised in the indictment. I should also ask you, Mr. Djordjevic, if you have had a chance to discuss the indictment with your duty counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have had the occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djordjevic, according to Rule 62(A) (iii) you may take up to 30 days to consider your plea but you may also enter your plea today. Have you decided which of the two options you wish to pursue today? Are you ready to enter your plea to the charges in the indictment today or do you wish to postpone this and then within the next 30 days have another Initial Appearance?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given that I have not resolved the issue of permanent counsel, I have decided, after talking to the duty counsel, to postpone my plea for 30 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. I will then instruct the registrar to schedule a date for a second Initial Appearance in which the accused will enter his final plea to the charges. This makes it easy because we can then proceed to the completion of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may raise a point? I'm not sure we had established yet whether -- we haven't read the indictment to him. I understand that he was willing to waive it but I don't know if we made that point on the record yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'll be perfectly willing to read out the points in the indictment or to just summarise them very briefly but I suppose that this is really not necessary in the circumstances, since he's going to plead again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's fine, Your Honour, if we take it up then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, before we conclude, I would like to ask you about your health and if you have anything to say, we can go into private session, if you so prefer. What I want to know is whether you are in good shape or whether you are in need of particular medical assistance or if there are any other conditions that the Court needs to be advised of before we move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I arrived here, I was examined by a general practitioner. It was established that there are no problems, and everything is all right as far as my accommodation is concerned and the staff employed there. There are no problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you have any points that you wish to raise at this moment regarding your detention? Is there any matter that you wish to raise at this point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Everything is fine, and I think that it is in compliance with the existing rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is there anything that the parties wish to bring up at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to indicate to the Court that typically we would make disclosure right away, but in the past when we've had temporary counsel appointed we found it more efficient to wait until we determine who the permanent counsel is going to be because we made disclosure and then it got lost or incompletely transferred. So once we are informed of who the permanent counsel will be, we will proceed immediately to make disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I was just going to raise that point because I believe that the rules require that you hand over the copies of the accompanying material to the accused 30 days after the Initial Appearance, but I suppose this is the final Initial Appearance they are talking about. Nevertheless, for the purpose of facilitating the accused's considerations of choosing his counsel, he may wish to be given a copy of the accompanying material, if that is possible, right away. And it also may be convenient for the duty counsel to have access to that material in order to discuss with him which of the counsels he may wish to choose. So, Mr. Prosecutor, if it can be done without too much trouble, I would prefer that you hand over the copies of the accompanying material to the accused and his duty counsel as soon as possible, and then I'm sure that the duty counsel will hand over that material immediately to the assigned counsel once we get that far, but I don't think there is any reason to prevent the accused from having access to this material. He needs all the time he can get.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree. One catch for the accused and whoever permanent counsel will be is that under my understanding, the time limit for filing motions begins to run for them when the disclosure is received. So duty counsel may receive the material tomorrow. The time limit starts running and permanent counsel may not come on until the day that motions are required to be filed. I just want to alert the accused and counsel to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Nevertheless, I think you should proceed with making these copies available to the accused. Any other matters to raise, yes, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, just two sentences. I have the same position as my learned friend from the Prosecution. I do believe that the disclosure should begin -- should start when the permanent counsel is appointed, given that the deadlines start running from the moment the supporting material is received. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. My point was that the accused will be in great need to see everything that is available at this moment to him as soon as possible, and if he wishes to raise any motions, of course, he will be aware that the time limit starts running from today and I assume that you will advise him properly to this effect so I think we should proceed the way I have suggested. There was one thing that I wanted to ask about to the Prosecution, and that relates to the proximity of this case with the trial against Milutinovic and others. And I would be curious to know if the Prosecution has any intention of filing a motion for joinder or rather rejoinder of this case to the Milutinovic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that has been discussed internally. We have not made a final decision. We are trying to weigh the logistical pros and cons of that matter. But that's something that we will make a final decision shortly. And we have a Pre-Defence Conference that's Friday in the remainder of the case with Judge Bonomy and I'm sure it's a matter we will talk about then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I realise the enormous difficulties in joining the case, but I just wanted to know if you had that intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: This concludes the business for today. This meeting is adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.44 p.m.
